items.title: 61428_Red Callender oral history interview
items.q: I said, 'Wow, that's wonderful, but I really would rather stay here and learn more about music.' Because I knew if I went with Duke, I'd never get to play my tuba and I'd never get to write.

ctx.x: Oh, immediately on going to that school you started with the tuba.

Immediately I started with the tuba. And, well, the alto horn; I played an alto horn, too. But the tuba was my love. I used to lay under our old Majestic radio and listen to Duke Ellington and Paul Whiteman (they used to broadcast every night, you know), and all I could hear was the tuba and the bass. At that time, Duke had a tuba, too. I imagine you have some of those old records.

items.title: 61428_Red Callender oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] You remind me of another musician I knew once, Mister Ellington... [INTERVIEWEE] Well, I understand what he meant.

ctx.x: No, I never did. And the reason being, when you played bass before the days of amplification, they had these giant bass drums, and the guys with big feet pounding on them -- and it's pretty difficult to really be heard. So that was one reason I didn't care for Dixieland music. The press rolls on the drums, they would swallow up all the bass notes. So I guess that's why I asked for $450, and I didn't get it. Well, I figured if I'm going to play this kind of music... You know, I'm still learning even in 1982, and…
You remind me of another musician I knew once, Mister Ellington, who used to call himself "an up-and-coming young bandleader," and that was in his seventies.

Well, I understand what he meant. Because you can play music... If I live to be 200... I've said this before. But you never can learn all there is to know. You only learn a little bit. So if you learn a little bit every day, you replenish a certain amount of knowledge. But there's no complete musicians. Some people might think they are, but they get carried away with themselves. You're never finished.
